cards.title: VPC: A Global Resource
cards.teaser: A GCP Virtual Private Cloud is a global resource — a single VPC can span every region on the planet. This is the opposite of AWS, where VPCs are regional. Understanding GCP's global VPC model is the foundation for everything else in GCP networking.

runs.text: In GCP, a
Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)

is a globally-scoped, software-defined network. You create one VPC and it automatically spans all GCP regions. VMs in us-central1 and VMs in asia-southeast1 can be in the same VPC and communicate over GCP's private backbone without touching the public internet.
Create a custom-mode VPC (the recommended type) with:

explanation.text:
# Create a custom-mode VPC (you define subnets explicitly)
gcloud compute networks create my-vpc \
  --subnet-mode=custom \
  --bgp-routing-mode=global

# Verify
gcloud compute networks describe my-vpc

runs.text: There are two subnet modes:

items.text: Auto mode

— GCP automatically creates one subnet per region using predefined /20 CIDR ranges from 10.128.0.0/9. Convenient for exploration; not recommended for production because ranges overlap with common on-prem address spaces.
Custom mode
— you define every subnet explicitly: region, CIDR block, and secondary ranges. Use this for all production workloads. You control the address plan.

runs.text: GCP VPC has important properties: it is
project-scoped
by default (each project gets a default VPC), but
Shared VPC
lets a host project share its VPC with service projects — a common pattern for large organizations that want centralized network administration.
A conceptual layout of a GCP VPC spanning regions:

GCP VPCs do not have an Internet Gateway resource like AWS does. Internet access for VMs is controlled by whether the VM has an external IP and what firewall rules allow. NAT for private instances is provided by Cloud NAT (a separate managed service).

A GCP VPC is one global network that stretches across every region. You put subnets inside it for specific regions. Unlike AWS where you'd need a VPC per region, one GCP VPC gives you global private connectivity out of the box.

cards.title: Subnets: Regional IP Ranges
cards.teaser: While the VPC is global, subnets are regional. Each subnet is an IP address range bound to one region. VMs get their internal IPs from subnet ranges. Understanding primary and secondary ranges is essential for GKE and other multi-address workloads.

runs.text: A
subnet

in GCP is a regional resource — it belongs to exactly one region (e.g., us-central1) within a VPC. Every VM instance must be placed in a specific zone within a region, and it receives an internal IP from the subnet's primary IP range.

explanation.text:
# Create a subnet in us-central1
gcloud compute networks subnets create prod-subnet-us \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --range=10.10.1.0/24 \
  --enable-private-ip-google-access

# Add a secondary range for GKE pods
gcloud compute networks subnets update prod-subnet-us \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --add-secondary-ranges=pods=10.20.0.0/14,services=10.24.0.0/20

runs.text: Key subnet properties:

items.text: Primary IP range
— the main CIDR block. VM internal IPs are allocated from here. Can be expanded (but not shrunk) after creation.
Secondary IP ranges
— additional ranges attached to the same subnet. GKE uses them for Pod IPs and Service IPs (alias IP ranges). A single VM can hold multiple IP aliases.
Private Google Access
— when enabled, VMs without external IPs can still reach Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, etc.) over the Google network. Enable on every production subnet.
Flow Logs
— optional per-subnet logging of network flows to Cloud Logging. Essential for security auditing and troubleshooting but adds cost.

runs.text: Subnets are
not
availability zones. A subnet in us-central1 spans all zones in us-central1 (us-central1-a, b, c, f). You place VMs in specific zones; they all share the regional subnet.
Choose non-overlapping CIDR ranges across subnets and with on-prem networks before connecting via VPN or Interconnect. RFC 1918 overlap is the most common pain point when migrating workloads to GCP.

Subnets are the actual IP address pools inside a VPC — one per region. VMs get their private IPs from the subnet's range. Secondary ranges let you assign extra IPs to the same VM (for GKE pods, for example).

cards.title: Firewall Rules: VPC-Level Ingress and Egress
cards.teaser: GCP firewall rules are stateful, VPC-scoped, and applied to VMs via network tags or service accounts — not subnet-level like AWS Security Groups. Getting the targeting model right is critical for both security and operational flexibility.

runs.text: GCP
firewall rules
are VPC-level constructs. They are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed) and apply to VM instances based on
targets
: network tags, service accounts, or all instances in the VPC.

explanation.text:
# Allow HTTP/HTTPS to VMs tagged 'web-server'
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-http \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS \
  --action=ALLOW \
  --rules=tcp:80,tcp:443 \
  --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 \
  --target-tags=web-server \
  --priority=1000

# Allow internal traffic within the VPC
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-internal \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS \
  --action=ALLOW \
  --rules=all \
  --source-ranges=10.0.0.0/8 \
  --priority=1000

runs.text: Firewall rule anatomy:

items.text: Direction
— INGRESS (incoming to VM) or EGRESS (outgoing from VM). Default: implicit DENY all ingress, ALLOW all egress.
Priority
— 0 (highest) to 65535 (lowest). Rules are evaluated in priority order; first match wins. Default rules are at priority 65534/65535.
Target
— which VMs the rule applies to. Options: all instances in VPC, instances with a specific
network tag
, or instances running a specific
service account
. Service account targeting is more secure (tags are user-mutable; service accounts are IAM-controlled).
Source / Destination
— for INGRESS: source IP ranges or source tags/service accounts. For EGRESS: destination IP ranges.

runs.text: Hierarchical Firewall Policies (organization- or folder-level) sit above VPC firewall rules in evaluation order. They allow security teams to enforce mandatory allow/deny rules that individual project firewall rules cannot override.

Firewall Rules Logging records each connection that matches a rule. Enable it on allow rules for sensitive resources (e.g., database-tier VMs) to get an audit trail of who connected and when. Disable on high-volume rules (e.g., internal load balancer health checks) to control cost.

GCP firewall rules live at the VPC level and target individual VMs using tags or service accounts. You write a rule that says 'allow port 443 to VMs tagged web-server' — not 'allow traffic to this subnet.' That flexibility means you can apply different rules to different VMs even when they share a subnet.

cards.title: Cloud Load Balancing: Global vs Regional
cards.teaser: GCP Cloud Load Balancing is not a single product — it is a family of load balancers across four dimensions: scope (global vs regional), traffic type (HTTP(S), TCP/SSL, UDP), and access (external vs internal). Choosing the wrong tier is one of the most common GCP architecture mistakes.

runs.text: GCP offers seven distinct load balancing products. The decision tree starts with three questions: Is the traffic external or internal? Is it HTTP(S) or TCP/UDP? Do you need a single global anycast IP?

explanation.text:
Load Balancer Type Comparison

┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
│ Load Balancer                │ Scope    │ Protocol │ Use Case                      │
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
│ Global External HTTP(S)      │ Global   │ HTTP/S   │ Web apps, APIs, Cloud CDN     │
│ Regional External HTTP(S)    │ Regional │ HTTP/S   │ Data residency compliance     │
│ External TCP/SSL Proxy       │ Global   │ TCP/SSL  │ Non-HTTP TCP, Websockets      │
│ External UDP/TCP Pass-through│ Regional │ UDP/TCP  │ Gaming, IoT (raw IP preserve) │
│ Internal HTTP(S)             │ Regional │ HTTP/S   │ Internal microservices        │
│ Internal TCP/UDP             │ Regional │ TCP/UDP  │ Internal non-HTTP traffic     │
│ Internal Regional Managed    │ Regional │ HTTP/S   │ Next-gen internal HTTP LB     │
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

runs.text: The
Global External HTTPS Load Balancer
is the flagship product and the most commonly used. Key properties:

items.text: Single global anycast IP
— traffic is routed to the nearest GCP edge PoP, then forwarded to the closest healthy backend region. Reduces latency for global users.
SSL/TLS termination at the edge
— encryption is terminated at GCP's edge network, not at the VM. Google-managed SSL certificates are automatically provisioned and renewed.
URL map routing
— route different paths or hostnames to different backend services (e.g., /api/* to one MIG, /static/* to Cloud Storage).
Backend types
— supports Managed Instance Groups (MIGs), NEGs (zonal, internet, serverless), GCS buckets, and more.

runs.text: The
Internal HTTPS Load Balancer
(Envoy-based) is the right choice for east-west traffic between microservices. It does not have an external IP and is only reachable from within the VPC or connected networks.

Network tier matters for load balancers. The Premium Tier uses Google's global backbone to route traffic between users and backends worldwide. The Standard Tier routes over the public internet after entering the local GCP region — lower cost but higher latency and no global load balancing.

GCP has seven load balancers and picking the right one comes down to: external or internal traffic, HTTP or raw TCP, and global or regional. The global HTTPS LB gives you one IP that works worldwide; internal HTTPS LB handles traffic inside the VPC between services.

cards.title: Cloud CDN: Edge Caching for HTTP(S)
cards.teaser: Cloud CDN sits in front of the Global External HTTPS Load Balancer and caches responses at Google's edge PoPs worldwide. The result is dramatically reduced origin load and lower latency for static and semi-static content.

runs.text: Cloud CDN is
not a standalone service

— it is a feature enabled on a Global External HTTPS Load Balancer backend service. You enable it per backend; it intercepts cacheable responses and stores them at Google's edge Points of Presence (PoPs) close to users.

explanation.text:
# Enable Cloud CDN on an existing backend service
gcloud compute backend-services update my-backend \
  --global \
  --enable-cdn

# Configure cache mode (CACHE_ALL_STATIC is the default)
gcloud compute backend-services update my-backend \
  --global \
  --cache-mode=CACHE_ALL_STATIC \
  --default-ttl=3600 \
  --max-ttl=86400

runs.text: Cache modes:

items.text: CACHE_ALL_STATIC
— automatically caches responses with cacheable content types (images, JS, CSS) and valid cache headers. Default and recommended starting point.
USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS
— only caches when the origin sets Cache-Control headers explicitly. Gives your application full control.
FORCE_CACHE_ALL
— caches all responses regardless of cache headers, overriding origin directives. Useful for legacy apps that don't set headers correctly. Be careful: caches Set-Cookie responses if not excluded.

runs.text: Cache invalidation (purging) can be done per URL or with wildcard paths:

explanation.text:
# Invalidate a specific path
gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache my-url-map \
  --path "/assets/*"

# Invalidate everything
gcloud compute url-maps invalidate-cdn-cache my-url-map \
  --path "/*"

runs.text: Cache key configuration lets you control what dimensions define a unique cached response — by default it is the full URL. You can include or exclude query parameters, headers (e.g., Accept-Language for localized content), and cookies.

Cloud CDN integrates with Cloud Armor. Security policies set on the backend service apply before the CDN cache — meaning Cloud Armor can block bad actors before a cached response is served, saving both compute and egress costs.

Cloud CDN is a switch you flip on a load balancer backend. Once enabled, Google caches your responses at edge locations worldwide. Users get content from the nearest PoP instead of waiting for your servers to respond.

cards.title: Cloud Armor: DDoS Protection and WAF
cards.teaser: Cloud Armor is GCP's DDoS mitigation and Web Application Firewall service. It attaches to the Global HTTPS Load Balancer and enforces security policies at the edge — before traffic reaches your backends or CDN cache.

runs.text: Cloud Armor security policies are collections of rules evaluated in priority order. Each rule specifies a
match condition
(IP ranges, headers, request attributes, or
CEL expressions
) and an
action
(allow, deny with HTTP status code, or throttle/rate limit).

explanation.text:
# Create a security policy
gcloud compute security-policies create my-waf-policy \
  --description="Production WAF policy"

# Block a specific IP range
gcloud compute security-policies rules create 1000 \
  --security-policy=my-waf-policy \
  --expression="inIpRange(origin.ip, '203.0.113.0/24')" \
  --action=deny-403

# Enable OWASP Top 10 pre-configured WAF rules
gcloud compute security-policies rules create 2000 \
  --security-policy=my-waf-policy \
  --expression="evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('xss-v33-stable')" \
  --action=deny-403

# Attach to a backend service
gcloud compute backend-services update my-backend \
  --global \
  --security-policy=my-waf-policy

runs.text: Cloud Armor features:

items.text: DDoS protection

— always-on, volumetric DDoS protection is included at no extra cost for Global HTTPS LBs. Cloud Armor Managed Protection Plus adds adaptive protection (ML-based attack detection) and advanced DDoS response.
Pre-configured WAF rules
— OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set equivalents for SQLi, XSS, LFI, RFI, RCE, and more. Versioned and maintained by Google.
Rate limiting
— throttle requests per IP, per user, or per custom key. Use to prevent credential stuffing and scraping.
Bot management
— reCAPTCHA Enterprise integration for distinguishing humans from bots at the edge.
Named IP lists
— managed lists of IP ranges for Tor exit nodes, known scanners, and commercial threat intelligence feeds.

runs.text: Cloud Armor rules use Google's Common Expression Language (CEL). This gives you expressive match conditions: evaluate request headers, cookies, request body length, and geographic origin (origin.region_code) in a single rule.

Cloud Armor is the doorman at Google's edge. You write rules that say 'block this IP range' or 'deny requests that look like SQL injection' and Google enforces them at the PoP nearest the attacker — before the traffic ever reaches your servers.

cards.title: VPC Service Controls: Security Perimeters
cards.teaser: VPC Service Controls (VPC SC) create a security perimeter around GCP services — preventing data from leaving the perimeter even if an IAM policy has been misconfigured. It is the primary defense against data exfiltration from compromised credentials.

runs.text: VPC Service Controls addresses a specific threat: an attacker who has obtained valid GCP credentials (e.g., from a compromised service account key) and is trying to exfiltrate data by calling GCP APIs from outside your trusted environment.
The core concept is a
service perimeter

: a boundary that defines which GCP projects and services are protected. API calls that would move data across the perimeter boundary (e.g., a BigQuery export from a perimeter project to a Cloud Storage bucket in a project outside the perimeter) are blocked — regardless of IAM permissions.

explanation.text:
VPC Service Controls Perimeter Concept:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Service Perimeter               │
  │                                         │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Project A│    │  Protected APIs   │  │
  │  │ (BigQuery│───▶│  (BigQuery,       │  │
  │  │  data)   │    │   GCS, Spanner)   │  │
  │  └──────────┘    └───────────────────┘  │
  │                                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │
           │  ✗ BLOCKED: data cannot exit perimeter
           │    unless access level is satisfied
           ▼
  External Request (even with valid IAM)

runs.text: Access levels let you define conditions under which cross-perimeter access is allowed:

items.text: IP-based access levels
— allow API calls only from specific corporate IP ranges or VPN exit nodes.
Device-based access levels
— require access only from corp-managed devices (via BeyondCorp / Chrome Enterprise).
Identity-based access levels
— restrict to specific user identities or groups.

runs.text: Perimeter bridges allow two separate perimeters to share data with each other without merging them. Service perimeter dry-run mode lets you audit what would be blocked before enforcing — critical because mis-configured perimeters can break legitimate workflows.

VPC Service Controls is not a replacement for IAM — it is a complement. IAM controls who can do what. VPC SC controls where API calls can come from and where data can go. Combine both for defense in depth.

VPC Service Controls builds a fence around your GCP projects and services. Even if an attacker steals a service account key, they cannot move your BigQuery data outside the fence because GCP checks both IAM permission AND 'is this request coming from inside the perimeter?'

cards.title: Private Service Connect: Private Connectivity to GCP Services
cards.teaser: Private Service Connect (PSC) lets VMs reach GCP managed services (like Cloud SQL, Vertex AI, or your own published services) via private IPs inside your VPC — no public IPs, no peering, no route leakage.

runs.text: Before PSC, the primary way to reach GCP APIs privately was
Private Google Access
— traffic still went to public googleapis.com IPs (though over Google's network). PSC takes this further: it creates a
private IP endpoint
inside your VPC that resolves to a GCP service. The IP is yours and lives in your subnet.

explanation.text:
# Create a PSC endpoint for Cloud Storage within your VPC
gcloud compute addresses create psc-storage-endpoint \
  --global \
  --purpose=PRIVATE_SERVICE_CONNECT \
  --addresses=10.10.1.100 \
  --network=my-vpc

gcloud compute forwarding-rules create psc-storage \
  --global \
  --address=psc-storage-endpoint \
  --target-google-apis-bundle=all-apis

runs.text: PSC has two main use cases:

items.text: Connecting to Google-published services

— access GCP APIs (all-apis bundle), specific services like Cloud SQL, or Vertex AI. The endpoint IP is in your VPC; DNS resolution returns your private IP, not the public googleapis.com address. Combined with VPC SC, traffic never leaves your controlled environment.
Connecting to producer services (third-party or cross-VPC)

— a producer (e.g., a SaaS provider or another team's project) publishes a service behind a PSC service attachment. You create a PSC endpoint in your VPC. Traffic flows through PSC without VPC peering — no route advertisement, no IP overlap concerns.

runs.text: PSC replaces older Private Service Access (VPC peering-based) for many use cases. The key advantages over peering: no transitive routing problems, no risk of IP range overlap causing peering failures, and the producer cannot see your VPC routes.

PSC endpoints are directional — the consumer initiates. The producer cannot initiate connections back into the consumer's VPC. This is a useful security property: a compromised managed service cannot laterally move into customer VPCs.

Private Service Connect gives you a private IP inside your own VPC that forwards to a GCP service. Instead of calling storage.googleapis.com on a public IP, you call 10.10.1.100 — which never leaves Google's fabric and stays inside your VPC's security controls.

cards.title: Cloud NAT: Outbound NAT for Private Instances
cards.teaser: Cloud NAT is a managed, software-defined Network Address Translation service. It lets VMs without external IPs make outbound internet connections — without a NAT gateway VM that you must manage, patch, and scale.

runs.text: GCP's security best practice is to create VMs without external IPs — they cannot be directly reached from the internet, and if compromised they cannot easily exfiltrate data. But most applications still need
outbound
internet access: to download packages, call third-party APIs, or pull container images. Cloud NAT provides this without a bastion VM.

explanation.text:
# Create a Cloud Router (required by Cloud NAT)
gcloud compute routers create my-router \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --region=us-central1

# Create a Cloud NAT config on the router
gcloud compute routers nats create my-nat \
  --router=my-router \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
  --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

runs.text: Key Cloud NAT properties:

items.text: Managed, not VM-based
— Cloud NAT runs on Google's network infrastructure. There is no NAT instance to size, HA-pair, or patch. It scales automatically with your workload.
Regional
— each Cloud NAT config is regional. You configure it per region, per network. VMs in us-central1 use the us-central1 NAT config.
Static or dynamic external IPs
— use auto-allocation (GCP manages the IPs) or specify reserved static external IPs. Use static IPs when you need to whitelist your egress IPs at third-party APIs.
Inbound connections not allowed
— Cloud NAT is egress-only. Unsolicited inbound connections to NATted VMs are still blocked by the VPC. This is unlike a self-managed NAT VM that could be misconfigured to forward inbound traffic.
Port allocation
— NAT uses source port mapping. Each VM gets a range of ports per external IP. Default is 64 ports per VM; increase if VMs make many concurrent outbound connections (e.g., high-concurrency proxies).

runs.text: Cloud NAT works with GKE nodes, Cloud Run VPC connectors, and Compute Engine VMs. For Cloud Run or Cloud Functions that need outbound internet access through a specific IP, deploy a VPC connector and route egress through Cloud NAT.

Cloud NAT is Google's managed way to let VMs talk to the internet without giving them public IPs. It's fully serverless — you configure it and Google handles scaling. VMs can call out; nothing from the internet can call in.

cards.title: Cloud Interconnect: Dedicated Lines to GCP
cards.teaser: Cloud Interconnect provides private, high-bandwidth, low-latency connections between your on-premises network and GCP — bypassing the public internet entirely. Two variants: Dedicated Interconnect for direct colocation connections, Partner Interconnect via a connectivity provider.

runs.text: Cloud Interconnect is for workloads where VPN latency and bandwidth are insufficient — large-scale data migrations, latency-sensitive hybrid applications, and high-throughput data pipelines between on-prem and GCP.

items.text: Dedicated Interconnect

— a physical cross-connect between your on-prem router and a Google-operated colocation facility. Provides 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits. You must have network equipment in (or connect to) one of Google's colocation facilities. Supports up to 8 circuits per interconnect connection (up to 800 Gbps aggregate).
Partner Interconnect

— you connect to a Google-approved service provider (e.g., AT&T, Equinix, Tata) who provides the physical layer. Available in 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps tiers. Use when you cannot physically reach a Google colocation facility or need lower bandwidth.

explanation.text:
# Verify your interconnect is ACTIVE
gcloud compute interconnects describe my-interconnect \
  --format='table(name,operationalStatus,linkType)'

# Create a VLAN attachment (links Interconnect to your Cloud Router)
gcloud compute interconnects attachments dedicated create my-vlan-attachment \
  --interconnect=my-interconnect \
  --router=my-router \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --bandwidth=BPS_10G \
  --vlan=100

runs.text: Interconnect traffic flows through a VLAN attachment to a Cloud Router, which exchanges routes with your on-prem router via BGP. This means your on-prem network learns VPC subnet routes and vice versa.
For 99.99% SLA, configure
redundant Interconnect connections
: two VLAN attachments in the same metro, each on separate physical circuits and edge routers. GCP's topology checker validates whether your configuration qualifies for the highest SLA tier.

Dedicated Interconnect traffic does not traverse the public internet, which means it does not count against internet egress costs. You pay for Interconnect port usage and VLAN attachment fees instead — typically lower cost at sustained high bandwidth.

Dedicated Interconnect is a physical cable from your office/data center to Google. Partner Interconnect is the same concept but through a carrier. Both bypass the internet entirely — useful when you need predictable high bandwidth and low latency between on-prem and GCP.

cards.title: Cloud VPN: IPsec Tunnels to On-Premises
cards.teaser: Cloud VPN creates encrypted IPsec tunnels between your on-prem network and GCP over the public internet. HA VPN (the recommended configuration) provides a 99.99% SLA with two active tunnels and automatic failover.

runs.text: Cloud VPN is simpler and cheaper than Interconnect but uses the public internet as the transport layer. Bandwidth is limited to the available internet bandwidth and latency is variable. Suitable for: dev/test environments, lower-bandwidth production workloads, and as a failover path for Interconnect.
Two VPN product types:

items.text: HA VPN

— two active/active tunnels per VPN gateway, each on a different external IP. Automatically failovers on tunnel failure. Provides 99.99% SLA. Requires a BGP-capable on-prem VPN gateway. This is the recommended configuration for all new deployments.
Classic VPN (legacy)
— single tunnel, 99.9% SLA, supports static routes and policy-based routing in addition to BGP. No longer recommended for new deployments.

explanation.text:
# Create an HA VPN gateway
gcloud compute vpn-gateways create my-ha-vpn \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --stack-type=IPV4_ONLY

# Create Cloud Router for BGP
gcloud compute routers create vpn-router \
  --network=my-vpc \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --asn=65001

# Create VPN tunnel (interface 0)
gcloud compute vpn-tunnels create tunnel-1 \
  --peer-address=203.0.113.1 \
  --vpn-gateway=my-ha-vpn \
  --vpn-gateway-interface=0 \
  --ike-version=2 \
  --shared-secret=MY_SHARED_SECRET \
  --router=vpn-router \
  --region=us-central1

runs.text: VPN and Cloud Router work together: Cloud Router runs BGP over the VPN tunnel. Your on-prem router advertises its subnets to GCP, and GCP advertises VPC subnets to on-prem. No static routes to maintain — the network self-heals when topology changes.

HA VPN uses active/active tunnels — both tunnels carry traffic simultaneously, doubling throughput compared to active/standby. If one tunnel fails, all traffic shifts to the surviving tunnel with sub-second detection via BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection).

Cloud VPN creates an encrypted tunnel from your office to GCP over the internet. HA VPN runs two tunnels at once so if one breaks, traffic keeps flowing. It's the go-to choice when you need private connectivity but Interconnect's cost or colocation requirement isn't justified.

cards.title: Network Endpoint Groups: Flexible Load Balancer Backends
cards.teaser: Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs) define collections of backends for a GCP load balancer by IP:port or by logical endpoint type. They unlock backends that aren't VMs in Managed Instance Groups — including serverless workloads, internet endpoints, and hybrid on-prem backends.

runs.text: A
Network Endpoint Group (NEG)

is an alternative backend type for GCP Load Balancers. Instead of pointing a backend service at a Managed Instance Group (which is a group of VMs), you point it at a NEG, which can represent many different kinds of endpoints.

items.text: Zonal NEG

— a set of VM IP:port combinations or GKE pod IP:port combinations within a zone. The GKE Container-native load balancing feature uses zonal NEGs to route directly to pod IPs, bypassing kube-proxy for lower latency and better visibility into backend health.
Internet NEG

— a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or IP that lives on the public internet. Lets you use a GCP load balancer as a front door for backends hosted outside GCP (on-prem, other clouds, CDN origins). Supports HTTPS backends.
Serverless NEG

— points to a Cloud Run service, App Engine app, or Cloud Functions function. Lets you put a Global HTTPS Load Balancer (with Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor) in front of serverless workloads — critical for custom domains, WAF protection, and CDN caching.
Hybrid connectivity NEG
— points to an on-premises backend reachable via Cloud Interconnect or VPN. Enables GCP load balancing across hybrid backends.
Private Service Connect NEG
— points to a PSC service attachment. Allows the load balancer to forward to services published via PSC.

explanation.text:
# Create a serverless NEG for a Cloud Run service
gcloud compute network-endpoint-groups create my-run-neg \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --network-endpoint-type=serverless \
  --cloud-run-service=my-service

# Add the NEG as a backend to a backend service
gcloud compute backend-services add-backend my-backend-svc \
  --global \
  --network-endpoint-group=my-run-neg \
  --network-endpoint-group-region=us-central1

runs.text: Container-native load balancing with GKE + Zonal NEGs reduces load balancing hops from three (LB -> node -> pod) to two (LB -> pod). This eliminates double-hop latency and gives health checks direct visibility into pod health rather than node health.

A NEG is a backend definition for a load balancer that isn't tied to a specific VM group. Serverless NEG means Cloud Run gets a load balancer. Internet NEG means external servers get a load balancer. Zonal NEG means GKE pods get routed to directly.

cards.title: Hybrid Connectivity: Interconnect vs VPN Decision Framework
cards.teaser: Cloud Interconnect and Cloud VPN both connect on-prem to GCP, but the right choice depends on bandwidth requirements, latency sensitivity, budget, and whether you can physically reach a Google colocation facility. Using the wrong one costs you either money or reliability.

runs.text: The decision between Interconnect and VPN is ultimately about the four dimensions of hybrid connectivity: bandwidth, latency, cost structure, and availability requirements.

explanation.text:
Hybrid Connectivity Decision Framework

┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Dimension            │ HA VPN                │ Partner Interconnect  │ Dedicated Interconnect│
├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Bandwidth            │ Up to ~3 Gbps         │ 50 Mbps – 50 Gbps     │ 10 Gbps – 200 Gbps   │
│ Latency              │ Variable (internet)   │ Low, consistent       │ Lowest, consistent   │
│ SLA                  │ 99.99% (HA VPN)       │ 99.9% – 99.99%        │ 99.9% – 99.99%       │
│ Physical requirement │ None                  │ Provider PoP          │ Google colo facility │
│ Setup time           │ Hours                 │ Days to weeks         │ Weeks to months      │
│ Cost model           │ Per-tunnel + data     │ Port + attachment      │ Port + attachment    │
│ Internet traversal   │ Yes (encrypted)       │ No                    │ No                   │
│ Recommended for      │ Dev/test, < 1 Gbps,   │ No colo access,       │ > 5 Gbps sustained,  │
│                      │ failover path         │ medium bandwidth      │ latency-critical     │
└──────────────────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

runs.text: A common pattern is to use both:
Dedicated Interconnect as the primary path
(for production workloads, low latency, high bandwidth) with
HA VPN as a backup
. Configure Cloud Router with MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator) values so traffic prefers the Interconnect path but automatically fails over to VPN if Interconnect goes down.
Key architectural principles:

items.text: Always use BGP with Cloud Router
— static routes don't scale and don't auto-heal. BGP via Cloud Router is the production standard for both VPN and Interconnect.
Plan for redundancy from day one
— single-tunnel VPN or single-circuit Interconnect will have planned and unplanned downtime. For business-critical workloads, two of everything in two different metros.
Address plan before you connect
— overlapping RFC 1918 ranges between on-prem and GCP VPC subnets cannot be routed. Map your entire address space before provisioning hybrid connectivity.

runs.text: Cross-Cloud Interconnect extends the same Dedicated Interconnect model to connect GCP directly to AWS or Azure — bypassing the public internet for multi-cloud architectures. The setup is the same as Dedicated Interconnect to on-prem but the far end is another cloud provider's Direct Connect or ExpressRoute endpoint.

Use VPN when you need hybrid connectivity quickly, cheaply, or for lower bandwidth. Use Interconnect when you need consistent high bandwidth, predictable low latency, and can justify the setup time and colocation requirements. Many production setups use both — Interconnect as primary, VPN as backup.
